2023 · NeurIPS 2023 · Benchmarks & Evals

Pick-a-Pic: An Open Dataset of User Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation

A public web app turns real text-to-image users into an open, half-million-pair preference dataset, and PickScore — a CLIP-based scorer trained on it — learns to predict those preferences well enough to beat the paper's own human baseline, then gets proposed as the new default metric for evaluating and ranking text-to-image models.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Collecting a large dataset of human preferences over model outputs is exactly the ingredient that made instruction-following language models work — InstructGPT and Anthropic's HH-RLHF both lean on large sets of comparisons scored by paid annotators — but that recipe had never been run in the open for text-to-image generation, and for a structural reason: companies running consumer image-generation products can log real user choices at scale, while everyone else is stuck either paying crowd workers to rate images they had no stake in, or falling back on older, prompt-oblivious metrics.

Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), still the default way papers report text-to-image quality, measures how close a batch of generated images sits to a batch of real ones in an Inception-net feature space — it never looks at the prompt at all — and it is conventionally scored against Microsoft COCO, a captioning dataset of ordinary photographs ("[a] man riding a bike past a train …") that looks nothing like what people actually type into an image generator ("[a] galactic eldritch squid towering over the planet Earth, stars, galaxies and nebulas in the background …").

The existing preference-style resources don't close the gap either. Simulacra Aesthetic Captions collects roughly 200,000 absolute aesthetic ratings, not pairwise comparisons. Lee et al. synthesize templated prompts across three challenge categories — count, color, and background ("[number] dogs") — have crowd workers label each generated image good or bad, and use the resulting 30,000 examples to train a scoring function (the paper does not say how many distinct prompts that covers). And two efforts concurrent with this one, HPS (Wu et al.) and ImageReward (Xu et al.), both rely on annotators judging prompts and images they had no hand in creating: HPS scrapes roughly 25,000 ratings (about 100,000 images) from Stability AI's own Discord channel, and ImageReward pays crowd workers for 136,892 examples over 8,878 prompts and never publicly releases the resulting dataset. Pick-a-Pic's premise is that the intrinsic motivation of a real user who wrote their own prompt and wants a specific image out of it is a meaningfully different — and more useful — training signal than an outside rater's judgment of someone else's prompt.

// how it works

The method

The mechanism is a public web app. A user types a prompt, the app generates two images from it, and the user is asked to select their preferred option or indicate a tie if they have no strong preference; the rejected image is then replaced with a freshly generated one and the loop continues until the user edits the prompt. Users authenticate via a Gmail or Discord account, explicitly consent to their interactions becoming part of a public dataset, and are capped at 1,000 interactions (periodically raised); the team additionally monitors activity logs and filters NSFW phrases to control quality. Before settling on this design, the authors piloted three annotation formats — 4 images with no ties, 2 images with no ties, 2 images with ties — and kept the third, which scored best on both user engagement and inter-rater agreement.

The images come from a handful of 2023-era backbones — Stable Diffusion 2.1, Dreamlike Photoreal 2.0 (a fine-tune of Stable Diffusion 1.5), and Stable Diffusion XL variants — sampled at different classifier-free guidance scales. As of the paper's writing the app had logged 968,965 rankings from 66,798 prompts and 6,394 users, but the reported experiments run on an earlier, NSFW-filtered snapshot: 583,747 training examples drawn from 37,523 prompts and 4,375 distinct users, plus a held-out slice of 1,000 prompts split evenly into 500 validation and 500 test examples (one sampled example per prompt per split, so no split shares a prompt with another).

What the raw preferences already support

Before any model is trained, the logged preferences already support two kinds of analysis on their own. To compare different settings of the same model, the authors take judgments between two images both generated by Stable Diffusion XL (Alpha) but at different classifier-free guidance scales, and compute a win/tie/lose ratio per scale — a guidance scale of 9 tends to beat a guidance scale of 3. To compare different models, they take judgments between Dreamlike Photoreal 2.0 and Stable Diffusion 2.1 outputs on shared prompts, and get a 53.5% / 35.2% / 11.2% split (Dreamlike wins / SD 2.1 wins / tie).

// which version this page follows

arXiv 2305.01569 has two versions. This page is built from v2 — the 23 Nov 2023 NeurIPS camera-ready, 12 pages — which is also what the "source ↗" link above resolves to. v2 differs from the original 10-page v1 (May 2023) in one number that matters: v1 reports PickScore's held-out preference-prediction accuracy as 70.2%; v2 adds a variance estimate over three training seeds and reports it as 70.5% ± 0.142. Every accuracy figure quoted below is v2's — treat a secondary source quoting 70.2% as citing the superseded preprint.

PickScore, the scoring function trained on top of the dataset, follows CLIP's architecture directly: a transformer text encoder and a transformer image encoder each map their input to a d-dimensional vector, and the score is their inner product scaled by CLIP's own learned temperature parameter T.

s(x, y) = Etxt(x) · Eimg(y) · T // x = prompt, y = image; E_txt, E_img are CLIP-style transformer encoders

The training objective adapts InstructGPT's reward-model loss to a two-way comparison. Given a prompt x, two images y₁ and y₂, and a preference vector p — [1,0] if y₁ is preferred, [0,1] if y₂ is preferred, [0.5,0.5] for a tie — the two raw scores are softmax-normalized into p̂, and the loss is the KL-divergence between p and p̂:

p̂i = exp s(x, yi)Σⱼ exp s(x, yj)     Lpref = Σᵢ pᵢ (log pᵢ − log p̂ᵢ) // batch-averaged with each example inverse-weighted by its prompt's frequency, so a few over-represented prompts can't dominate the gradient

PickScore finetunes CLIP-H (starting from OpenCLIP weights) on the training split for 4,000 steps — batch size 128, learning rate 3e-6 with a 500-step warmup then linear decay — which the paper reports finishes in under an hour on 8 A100 GPUs, with no hyperparameter search. Model selection uses validation accuracy (with the tie option disabled) checked every 100 steps, keeping the best checkpoint. A separate objective that adds in-batch negatives — closer to CLIP's original contrastive loss — is tried in the appendix and found worse (65.2% vs. the main objective's accuracy).

// what they found

The results

On the task PickScore was trained for — predicting which of two images a real Pick-a-Pic user preferred — it comes out ahead of everything else the paper tests, including people. The evaluation metric awards one point for an exact match with the user's label, half a point when either the label or the prediction (but not both) is a tie, and zero otherwise; every model except the human raters gets its own tie-probability threshold, selected on the validation set and then frozen for the test set (human experts are simply allowed to say "tie" directly, with no threshold to tune).

ModelAccuracy
Random56.8
Aesthetics predictor56.8
CLIP-H (zero-shot)60.8
ImageReward (concurrent)61.1
HPS v1 (concurrent)66.7
Human Expert68.0
PickScore (ours)70.5 ± 0.142

All seven rows are on the same 500-example test set. Random and the aesthetics predictor land exactly tied at 56.8%; the two concurrent scoring functions sit in between — ImageReward at 61.1%, and HPS at 66.7% (this is HPS v1, Wu et al.'s original "Better Aligning Text-to-Image Models with Human Preference," not the later HPS v2 that appears elsewhere on this map as a separate paper). PickScore's 70.5% ± 0.142 is the table's maximum, ahead of the 68.0% human-expert row — the paper's "superhuman" headline.

The paper's second line of results turns from predicting individual preferences to ranking whole models — arguably the stronger case for PickScore. Against 100 MS-COCO captions rendered by 9 models (3 backbones × guidance scales {3, 6, 9}), the model ranking induced by FID correlates with the ranking induced by human experts at Spearman R = −0.900 — negatively, and "surprisingly" in the paper's own word, since FID is oblivious to the prompt and the paper argues one would expect zero correlation, not a strong negative one; their hypothesis is that higher guidance scales look better to people but push the generated distribution further from COCO's photos, which is exactly what FID penalizes. PickScore's win-rate ranking on the same 9 models correlates with human experts at Spearman R = 0.917.

A second, larger-scale check replaces MS-COCO captions with the real preferences already in Pick-a-Pic: all 14,000 collected test-set preferences, spanning 45 models (four backbones at different guidance scales), are converted into Elo ratings, and the process is repeated 50 times with reshuffled example order to get a mean and standard deviation. PickScore's Elo ratings correlate with real users' Elo ratings at 0.790 ± 0.054 — ahead of HPS v1 (0.670 ± 0.071), ImageReward (0.492 ± 0.086), and CLIP-H (0.313 ± 0.075) — the cleanest margin in the paper, in the sense of resting on the most models, the most real (not proxy) preferences, and an explicit variance estimate over 50 reshuffles.

Finally, Section 6 uses PickScore as a re-ranker rather than a judge: for 100 Pick-a-Pic test prompts, the authors generate 100 Dreamlike Photoreal 2.0 images per prompt (5 random seeds × 20 prompt-embellishment templates, including the plain, unmodified "null" template) and keep the single image PickScore scores highest. Human raters then prefer PickScore's pick over a randomly chosen image from the null-template pool 71.4% of the time, over a randomly chosen image from the full template pool 82.0% of the time, over the aesthetics predictor's pick 85.1% of the time, and over CLIP-H's pick 71.3% of the time. In a non-human check on the same setup, PickScore's picks score higher on the aesthetics metric than CLIP-H's picks 68.5% of the time, and score higher on CLIP-H's own text-alignment metric than the aesthetics predictor's picks 90.5% of the time.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The dataset side of this paper is close to unimpeachable: a genuinely open, half-million-example release built from motivated real users rather than crowd workers, with a clean no-prompt-overlap train/val/test split. The parts worth pushing on are the "superhuman" claim and the second-order consequences of turning a preference-trained scorer into the field's recommended evaluation metric.

"Superhuman" compared to what, exactly? The 68.0% human baseline in Table 1(b) comes from a specific, disclosed source: footnote 9 says the authors "use friends and colleagues of the authors for expert human annotation." That's not a broad or blinded comparison group, and the paper is careful to scope the claim narrowly in its own prose — it argues that beating this baseline means outperforming "a human annotator that is oblivious to the original user's context, idea, and motivation," not beating an ordinary text-to-image user, since the ground-truth labels come from users who wrote their own prompts and know what they wanted. That's a real and interesting distinction, but it is a much narrower claim than the word "superhuman" advertises on its own. The paper's acknowledgments thank at least nine named people — Roni Herman, Or Honovich, Avia Efrat, Samuel Amouyal, Tomer Ronen, Uri Shaham, Maor Ivgi, Itay Itzhak, and Illy Sachs, plus unnamed "other friends and colleagues" — "for their contribution to the annotation endeavor of this project," so the panel is not tiny, but the paper never says how many of them produced the 68.0% figure specifically, how the 500 test judgments were distributed across them, or what their inter-annotator agreement was.

Whose preferences, exactly? The web app was promoted through Twitter, Facebook, Discord, and Reddit, so both the training data and the "human preference" being predicted describe a self-selected community of 2023 text-to-image hobbyists generating from a handful of specific checkpoints (Stable Diffusion 2.1, Dreamlike Photoreal 2.0, SDXL Alpha variants) — not preferences in general. The paper's own Limitations section acknowledges NSFW content, users making "judgments without due care," and that "the preferences of users may include biases that may be reflected in the collected data" — but it doesn't discuss whether this specific, self-selected population's taste generalizes to a broader or more diverse set of image-generation users.

The tie-threshold asymmetry. Every model row in Table 1(b) — including PickScore — gets a tie-probability threshold selected on the validation set and then applied to the test set: a one-parameter calibration step tuned directly against the metric being reported. Human experts get no equivalent treatment; they are simply allowed to indicate a tie whenever they see one. This isn't obviously unfair to PickScore (a continuous score genuinely needs a threshold to produce a discrete tie/no-tie call, which a person doesn't), but it does mean the PickScore-vs-Human-Expert comparison in Table 1(b) is not a comparison of two systems evaluated identically — one side gets a free, metric-matched calibration pass and the other doesn't. The paper states the asymmetry plainly ("For human experts, we do not perform tie selection and explicitly allow them to select a tie"), it just never discusses what that difference in treatment does to the comparison.

The circularity risk. Sections 5–6 recommend PickScore as the field's evaluation metric and demonstrate it works as a re-ranking signal, selecting the best of 100 generations per prompt. Once future text-to-image models are optimized — even implicitly, through this kind of ranking-based selection — to score well on PickScore, PickScore stops being an independent read on what real users prefer and starts measuring correlation with its own training-time idiosyncrasies (the four 2023-era backbone models behind the Elo experiment's 45 checkpoints, and one self-selected user population). This is the standard Goodhart's-Law risk for any learned metric proposed as an optimization target, and the paper doesn't discuss it, even though Section 6 already demonstrates the exact mechanism (ranking generations by PickScore) that would trigger it.

An ambiguous "five times larger" claim. In the Related Work discussion, the paper states that "Pick-a-Pic is more than five times larger than the data used to train HPS and ImageReward." A few sentences earlier in the same discussion (not the same paragraph), it gives ImageReward's training set as 136,892 examples, and describes HPS only as scraping "about 25,000 human ratings (which include about 100,000 images)." The problem is which of Pick-a-Pic's own printed sizes the claim is measured against — the paper gives several: 583,747 training examples, the set actually used in this paper's reported experiments (§2); 968,965 — "we have gathered 968,965 rankings which originated from 66,798 prompts and 6,394 users" — from the same §2 "Statistics" paragraph, describing the live collection at time of writing rather than the frozen experimental snapshot; and, per footnote 2, "more than one million examples" in an already-released updated version. Against ImageReward's 136,892, the 583,747 figure gives only ≈4.3× — short of "more than five times" — while 968,965 gives ≈7.1× and the >1,000,000 figure clears it even more comfortably; against HPS's own operands, every one of Pick-a-Pic's size readings clears five times easily. So the claim is defensible under the paper's own larger figures for Pick-a-Pic, and only comes up short under the narrower (and arguably most relevant, since it's the set this paper's own experiments actually run on) 583,747 reading. Not resolvable from the paper alone — the ambiguity, not a settled error, is the finding.

baselines

Reasonably complete for its era — random, an aesthetics predictor, zero-shot CLIP-H, and both concurrent works (HPS v1, ImageReward) are all included, and PickScore beats every one of them on Table 1(b)'s test set — but every model baseline gets a validation-tuned tie threshold that the human baseline neither needs nor receives — an asymmetry the paper states plainly but never discusses the effect of.

contamination

No classical train/test leakage — the 1,000-prompt validation/test split shares no prompt with training, one example per prompt per split — but a distributional version of the same risk: PickScore is trained and evaluated entirely inside one self-selected 2023 web-app community's taste over four specific model backbones (Section 5's own count).

what's missed

Annotator count and inter-annotator agreement for the 68.0% human-expert baseline; any check of whether PickScore's edge over that baseline survives outside its training-time user population; and any discussion of what happens to PickScore's evaluation numbers once models are explicitly optimized against it, despite Section 6 already showing PickScore works as a selection/ranking target.

would raise confidence

A second, disjoint preference population (e.g. paid crowd workers under the same two-image, ties-allowed protocol) run against the same 500 test prompts, to see whether "superhuman" and the correlation numbers hold outside the web app's self-selected cohort; and a follow-up measuring PickScore's own calibration once a generator is trained or ranked specifically to please it.

// bottom line

The dataset is the paper's most durable contribution — an open, real-user preference resource that didn't exist before it. The "superhuman" scoring result is real but narrower than it sounds once you read footnote 9, and the case for PickScore as a replacement evaluation metric is genuinely strong on the correlation numbers (0.917 vs. −0.900 against human MS-COCO rankings; 0.790 vs. ≤0.670 Elo correlation with real users) while carrying an unaddressed circularity risk the moment models start optimizing against it — which the paper's own ranking experiment already shows is possible.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. Pick-a-Pic is the first large (583,747-example) open pairwise text-to-image preference dataset built from real, self-motivated web-app users rather than crowd workers or scraped Discord logs — closing a gap that InstructGPT-style RLHF work in text already had and text-to-image didn't.
  2. PickScore, a CLIP-H model finetuned on it with an InstructGPT-style pairwise KL objective, predicts held-out preferences at 70.5% ± 0.142 (this is v2's figure; the original arXiv v1 reported 70.2%) — ahead of the paper's 68.0% human baseline, though that baseline draws on an unspecified subset of the authors' friends and colleagues (at least nine are named in the acknowledgments) and is evaluated without the validation-tuned tie threshold every model baseline gets.
  3. The paper's second contribution — recommending PickScore as a replacement for FID-over-MS-COCO — rests on real evidence (0.917 vs. −0.900 correlation with human MS-COCO rankings; 0.790 vs. ≤0.670 Elo correlation with real users) but bakes in a circularity risk once models start optimizing against PickScore itself, a mechanism Section 6's own re-ranking results already demonstrate is available.
